## TL;DR

Stale `running` rows in the durable handoff-status store no longer block the board. `GET /api/tasks/:id/handoff-status` and `repoos handoff-status` reconcile each read against whether a handoff slot is actually live and whether the task has moved on (for example into `review` with a newer review pass). Orphaned records persist as `superseded` with a reason. Live handoffs that exceed `HANDOFF_DEADLINE_MS` stay `running` but return `stale: true`, and the card appends “stale” on the checks line. The task watchdog runs the same reconciliation every tick so records clear without waiting for a UI poll.

## Work and rationale

The incident on #1080 and #1070 was a split brain between three signals: the task was in `review` with a green verdict and `repoos landable` ready, while `handoff-status` still said `running` / step `validate` and the review card treated that like an active post-review check. `finishHandoffStatus` only runs when the finalization pipeline completes; if the worker releases the handoff slot without writing a terminal status—reload mid-validate, a parallel review pass, watchdog activity, or a abandoned waiter—the JSON file could sit at `running` indefinitely. The UI trusted that file directly (`handoffInFlight`, `reviewChecksRunning` on `TaskCard`).

The fix keeps `readHandoffStatus` as the raw store for writers and adds `reconcileHandoffStatus` for readers. Reconciliation superses when `handoffLive` is false and the task is already in `review`, when there is no live process on an `active` task, or when a stored review report’s `at` timestamp is newer than the handoff’s `startedAt` while the task is in `review`. Superseded rows keep their attempt metadata but clear `progress` so the card stops showing phantom validate work. When the slot is still live but elapsed time exceeds the same deadline the handoff wrapper uses, the API returns `stale: true` without persisting—covering acceptance criterion 2 without racing a process that may still be unwinding.

Wiring: `getTaskHandoffStatus` passes task status, runner `isHandoffInFlight` / `hasPendingHandoff`, and the latest review `at` into reconciliation. `TaskWatchdog.checkNow` calls the same helper for every `active` and `review` task whose on-disk state is still `running`, so CLI clients and the board converge even without opening the drawer. On the UI side, `handoffInFlight` treats `superseded` as terminal; `task-card-status` ignores superseded state for the checks lifecycle; `formatChecksCardLine` accepts `stale` and prints it after elapsed time; pipeline and drawer pass through the flag.

## Approaches tried

The first option considered was clearing the file to `not_requested` when the slot was empty. That would have made `handoff-status` lie about history and complicated engineer outcome deduplication. `superseded` preserves the attempt boundary and gives humans a reason string. Client-only filtering in Vue was rejected because `repoos handoff-status` and other API consumers would still see `running`; server reconciliation keeps one source of truth.

## Challenges and blockers

`handoff-status.ts` cannot import `HANDOFF_DEADLINE_MS` from `handoff.ts` without a circular import, so reconciliation accepts `staleAfterMs` from callers (`HANDOFF_DEADLINE_MS` on the route and watchdog). The default inside the module matches the same 30-minute formula for unit tests that do not load the handoff module.

No human verification on a live #1080-class board was possible in this session; behavior is covered by table-driven store tests and the existing landable/card tests, which now receive reconciled API data when polled.

## Key learnings

Durable progress stores need the same “is anything actually running?” reconciliation as check-gate locks. Persisting `running` is correct for reload survival, but every consumer that gates merge readiness must read through a reconcile step keyed off process/slot ownership, not the file alone. Flagging `stale` separately from `superseded` lets the UI warn on overdue live work without falsely clearing a slot the server still owns.
